lead: Energy is conserved; entropy is not. In every real process the total entropy of the system plus its surroundings rises, and the amount it rises by is the entropy generated, S_gen. This one inequality decides which processes are possible, separates the best possible machine from the actual one, and shows where a plant is destroying quality of energy. Engineers use it to judge heat exchanger designs, steam plant performance and any claim of a new, super-efficient engine.
prereq: You need: 3.7 for dS = δQ_rev/T, and 3.3 for what makes a process irreversible.

sections.h3: The principle written as an equation

blocks.text: For any process between state 1 and state 2, reversible or not, the entropy account reads as follows.

blocks.where: ΔS_system is the entropy change of the system in kJ/K, equal to S₂ − S₁; ΔS_surroundings is the entropy change of everything outside the system, in kJ/K; S_gen is the entropy generated during the process, in kJ/K; the sum is never negative.

blocks.text: The equality holds only for a fully reversible process. Every real process gives a strict greater-than. S_gen is not a property of the system; it is a quantity produced along the path, and it depends on how the process is carried out.

Seal the system and its surroundings into one box and you have an isolated system. For it the statement becomes: the entropy of an isolated system increases in every real process and stays constant only in a reversible one. It never falls. That is the second law stated in entropy words.

Compare this with the first law. The first law says energy is conserved, so the energy account always balances to zero. The second law says the entropy account does not balance to zero — it always leaves a positive remainder. Nature keeps books that never close.

sections.h3: S_gen measures how irreversible the process is

blocks.text: S_gen is a quantitative measure of irreversibility. Large S_gen means a badly irreversible process; zero means a reversible one. Four sources account for almost every case you will meet.
Heat through a finite temperature difference is the commonest. When Q kilojoules cross from a body at T_hot to a body at T_cold, both in kelvin:

blocks.where: Q is the heat in kJ passing from the hot body to the cold body; T_cold and T_hot are in K; S_gen is in kJ/K. The bracket is positive because T_cold < T_hot, so a wider gap or a larger Q creates more entropy.

blocks.text: A reversible adiabatic process has Q = 0 and no friction or mixing, so S_gen = 0 and ΔS = 0. Such a process is called isentropic — same entropy. On a T-s diagram the ideal gas turbine or compressor is drawn as a vertical line.

sections.h3: The criterion for a spontaneous change

blocks.text: The same inequality answers a different question: will this change happen on its own? For a closed system held at constant internal energy U and constant volume V, with no help from outside, the answer is yes only if dS ≥ 0. Entropy climbs to a maximum, and that maximum is the equilibrium state.

Only a few universities ask for this form. At constant temperature and volume the criterion is written with the Helmholtz function, at constant temperature and pressure with the Gibbs function; both are built from entropy and belong to Unit 4.

A positive ΔS says the process can happen, not that it happens quickly. The conversion of diamond to graphite has a positive ΔS at room conditions and you will not see it happen in your lifetime. Thermodynamics gives direction, never rate.

Every kJ/K of entropy generated makes T₀ × S_gen of work unavailable, where T₀ is the surroundings temperature in K. Unit 4 turns this into lost work, W_lost = T₀ S_gen, and into exergy, the part of energy still useful.

figure.caption: Heat crossing a finite temperature gap always creates entropy: the hot body loses 0.200 kJ/K and the cold body gains 0.333 kJ/K, so 0.133 kJ/K is newly created and cannot be recovered.

spec.title: Entropy created when heat crosses a temperature gap
spec.aria: One hundred kilojoules flows from a 500 K body to a 300 K body; the hot body loses 0.200 kJ/K of entropy, the cold body gains 0.333 kJ/K, leaving a net creation of 0.133 kJ/K.

examples.question: In an insulated vessel, 2 kg of water at 80 °C is mixed with 3 kg of water at 20 °C. Take cp = 4.187 kJ/kg·K and treat it as constant. Find the final mixture temperature and the total entropy change, and state whether the mixing is reversible. (8 marks)
steps: Convert to kelvin: T₁ = 80 + 273 = 353 K, T₂ = 20 + 273 = 293 K.
The vessel is insulated and no work crosses the boundary, so the heat given up by the hot water equals the heat taken by the cold water: m₁cp(T₁ − T_f) = m₂cp(T_f − T₂). The cp cancels.
Entropy change of the hot water: ΔS₁ = m₁cp ln(T_f/T₁) = 2 × 4.187 × ln(317/353) = 8.374 × (−0.10757) = −0.9008 kJ/K.
Entropy change of the cold water: ΔS₂ = m₂cp ln(T_f/T₂) = 3 × 4.187 × ln(317/293) = 12.561 × (0.07873) = +0.9889 kJ/K.
The vessel is insulated, so the surroundings change by zero. Total: ΔS_total = −0.9008 + 0.9889 = +0.0882 kJ/K = S_gen.
The total is positive, so the mixing is irreversible and allowed by the second law. Warm water giving heat to cold water is exactly the finite-temperature-gap source of entropy.
examples.answer: Final temperature 317 K (44 °C) and total entropy change +0.0882 kJ/K; positive, so the mixing is irreversible and possible.
examples.check:
import math
m1, T1 = 2.0, 353.0
m2, T2 = 3.0, 293.0
cp = 4.187
Tf = (m1*T1 + m2*T2)/(m1 + m2)
dS1 = m1*cp*math.log(Tf/T1)
dS2 = m2*cp*math.log(Tf/T2)
print(round(Tf, 2))
print(round(dS1, 4))
print(round(dS2, 4))
print(round(dS1 + dS2, 4))

traps: ΔS of the system alone may be negative — freezing water and compressing gas both do it. Only system plus surroundings is guaranteed non-negative, so write the full account before you conclude anything.
S_gen is in kJ/K, not kJ. Dividing Q by a temperature in °C gives nonsense; convert to kelvin first.
A reversible adiabatic process is isentropic (ΔS = 0). A reversible isothermal process is not: ΔS = Q/T is finite. Do not label every reversible process isentropic.
When the vessel is not insulated, the surroundings' entropy change must be added with its sign. Many answers lose marks by silently dropping it.
A positive ΔS says the process can happen, not that it happens quickly. Direction comes from thermodynamics; rate comes from kinetics.

quiz.q: State the principle of increase of entropy as one equation and define every term with its unit.
quiz.a: ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings = S_gen ≥ 0, all in kJ/K: ΔS_system = S₂ − S₁ of the system, ΔS_surroundings the change of everything outside it, and S_gen the entropy created, which is zero only for a reversible process.

quiz.q: For which kind of process is S_gen exactly zero?
quiz.a: A fully reversible process. A reversible adiabatic process also has ΔS = 0 and is called isentropic.

quiz.q: Water in a freezer loses entropy as it turns to ice. Does this break the second law?
quiz.a: No. The freezer's refrigerant and compressor reject more entropy to the room than the water loses. ΔS_water + ΔS_surroundings > 0; only the total is protected.

quiz.q: 50 kJ of heat flows from a body at 400 K to a body at 300 K. Find the entropy generated.
1 kg of water at 90 °C is mixed with 2 kg at 30 °C in an insulated vessel. Take cp = 4.187 kJ/kg·K. Find the final temperature and the total entropy change.
A gas is compressed isothermally from 100 kPa to 500 kPa and ΔS of the gas is negative. A student claims the second law is violated. What is missing from the argument?
quiz.a: The system's entropy may fall. Work is supplied and heat is rejected to the surroundings, whose entropy rises by at least as much. Check ΔS_sys + ΔS_surr = S_gen ≥ 0; for a reversible isothermal compression S_gen = 0 and the total is exactly zero.

quiz.q: 100 kJ leaves a 500 K body. In case A it goes directly to a 300 K body. In case B a reversible engine works between the same two bodies and the same 100 kJ leaves the hot body. Compare the entropy generated.
quiz.a: Direct: S_gen = 100(1/300 − 1/500) = 0.1333 kJ/K. With the reversible engine S_gen = 0, because Q_h/T_h = Q_c/T_c and there is no friction; part of the 100 kJ leaves as work, so less heat reaches the cold body. Case A destroys 0.1333 kJ/K worth of energy quality.

quiz.q: Why is a reversible adiabatic process called isentropic?
quiz.a: Because δQ = 0 and there is no internal irreversibility, so ΔS = ∫δQ_rev/T = 0. Entropy stays constant: iso (same) + entropic (entropy).

beyond: Not for the exam. In plant practice, S_gen is the number behind second law efficiency and exergy audits: a boiler that creates 2 kJ/K per kg of steam is throwing away work that a better-matched heat exchanger could recover. Modern curricula add entropy generation minimisation and the Bejan number to design heat exchangers and solar collectors. Researchers apply the same inequality to living systems and to data centres, where the entropy generated per unit of waste heat rejected is now audited in J/K. Search for entropy generation number, Gouy-Stodola theorem and exergy destruction to go further.
